clinicalPearls: A cutaneous angiosarcoma that arises within a chronically lymphoedematous limb, classically described after post-mastectomy arm lymphoedema but reported in any longstanding lymphoedema including congenital and filarial forms.
The latency is long, typically around a decade from the onset of chronic lymphoedema to tumour appearance.
Early lesions are subtle violaceous or red-blue macules, papules or bruise-like patches that are easily mistaken for simple ecchymosis on an oedematous limb.
Lesions are frequently multifocal, with satellite nodules that enlarge, coalesce, ulcerate and bleed.
Diagnosis rests on full-thickness incisional biopsy with immunohistochemistry demonstrating endothelial markers such as CD31, CD34, ERG and factor VIII-related antigen.
The tumour is aggressive with a strong tendency to early haematogenous metastasis, particularly to the lungs.
Wide surgical excision, often amputation, is the mainstay of treatment, with radiotherapy and chemotherapy as adjuncts, yet outcomes remain poor.
Any new or changing pigmented or violaceous lesion on a chronically swollen limb should prompt urgent biopsy rather than reassurance.
reference.pathophysiology: Stewart-Treves syndrome represents malignant transformation of vascular endothelium within a field of chronic lymphoedema. Persistent stasis of protein-rich lymph is thought to create a locally immunocompromised, immunologically privileged microenvironment in which impaired immune surveillance, sustained tissue remodelling, aberrant lymphangiogenic and angiogenic signalling, and chronic inflammation promote accumulation of oncogenic changes in endothelial cells. The result is a high-grade angiosarcoma composed of atypical, anastomosing vascular channels lined by malignant endothelium that infiltrates dermis and subcutis. The same predisposing stasis explains why the tumour tends to be multifocal across the affected territory.
additionalDifferentials: traumatic bruising or haematoma on an oedematous limb
recurrent or metastatic cutaneous breast carcinoma
benign vascular tumours such as haemangioma or pyogenic granuloma
additionalInvestigations: incisional skin biopsy with endothelial immunohistochemistry (CD31, CD34, ERG)
magnetic resonance imaging of the affected limb to delineate extent
staging computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis
positron emission tomography for occult multifocal or metastatic disease
sentinel or regional nodal assessment where indicated
review of prior oncological history and radiotherapy fields
redFlags: new violaceous, red-blue or bruise-like cutaneous lesions on a chronically lymphoedematous limb
rapid growth, ulceration or spontaneous bleeding of a skin lesion
multifocal or coalescing nodules over the affected territory
systemic symptoms or respiratory features suggesting pulmonary metastasis
a non-healing lesion previously dismissed as bruising or infection
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is poor: Stewart-Treves angiosarcoma is aggressive, frequently multifocal and metastasises early, so five-year survival is low even after radical surgery. Early recognition and wide excision offer the only realistic chance of prolonged survival.
pitfalls: mistaking early lesions for bruising, cellulitis or benign vascular change and delaying biopsy
taking an inadequate or superficial biopsy that misses the malignant endothelium
underestimating multifocality and performing insufficiently wide excision
failing to stage for pulmonary metastasis at presentation
attributing the swelling and skin change solely to the pre-existing lymphoedema

DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
management: Perform a thorough imaging workup for occult regional and distant disease at presentation, given the tendency to multifocality and early hematogenous spread.
Wide surgical excision is the treatment of choice when the disease is resectable, though even negative margins do not reliably prevent local recurrence.
Consider amputation, including shoulder disarticulation or hemipelvectomy as anatomically appropriate, when extremity disease cannot be adequately controlled with limb-sparing excision.
Consider postoperative radiotherapy in essentially all resected cases to improve local control, with retrospective data suggesting a survival benefit.
Recognize poor wound healing in the chronically lymphedematous limb as a recurring barrier to limb-sparing surgery.
Use systemic therapy with anthracycline-based or taxane-based regimens, to which this angiosarcoma variant is relatively chemosensitive, at least initially.
In the metastatic setting, use chemotherapy and radical radiotherapy with palliative intent, recognizing that neither has been shown to improve overall survival.
Regard VEGF-pathway antiangiogenic or targeted approaches as an area for specialist-directed, trial-informed therapy rather than an established treatment line for this disease.
Sequence localized, resectable disease as surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy, and reserve systemic therapy plus palliative radiotherapy for unresectable or metastatic disease.
Note there is no universally accepted staging system for this tumor, limiting sequencing to a resectable versus unresectable/metastatic framework.
Maintain surveillance chest imaging and close clinical follow-up of the affected limb and lymphedematous field after treatment, given the high metastatic potential.
Pursue prompt re-biopsy of any new violaceous, bruise-like, or nodular change in the limb after treatment rather than reassurance.

Refer promptly to a center with soft-tissue sarcoma and radiation oncology expertise for surgical and radiotherapy planning, and to medical oncology whenever systemic therapy or clinical trial consideration is warranted.
Involve specialists early once the diagnosis is suspected rather than pursuing a period of watchful observation, given generally poor reported outcomes.
